result.summary: Demeter nurses Metaneira's son Demophoon and tries to make him immortal in the fire, but Metaneira interrupts and the gift is lost. Demeter reveals herself and orders a temple at Eleusis, then withholds the harvest in grief until Zeus sends Iris to summon her.

scenes.title: Demeter nurses Demophoon
scenes.summary: Demeter takes the child and secretly anoints him with ambrosia and hides him in the fire at night. Metaneira spies and cries out in fear.
scenes.stakes: Demophoon would gain immortality; Metaneira fears for her son's life.

scenes.title: The goddess revealed
scenes.summary: Angered, Demeter drops the child, declares the immortality lost, and orders a temple and rites. She shows her true form and leaves, while the household tends the crying boy.
scenes.stakes: Demophoon loses the chance at deathlessness; Metaneira faces the wrath of a goddess.

scenes.title: Celeus builds the temple
scenes.summary: At dawn Celeus hears the story, assembles the people and has the temple and altar built.
scenes.stakes: The family fears the goddess's anger.

scenes.title: Famine and Iris's summons
scenes.summary: Demeter, pining for her daughter, causes a famine. Zeus sends Iris to call her to Olympus.
scenes.stakes: Mankind faces extinction by famine and the gods lose their sacrifices.

notable_quotes.reason: Demeter's rebuke of mortals' blindness to their fate.
Demeter declares her identity and importance.

analysis.text: Mortals cannot gain immortality; human fear and limits defeat divine gifts, explaining why death is unavoidable.
The passage gives an origin for the Eleusinian temple and its mysteries, central to Greek religion.

legacy.text: The Eleusinian Mysteries at Eleusis lasted nearly two thousand years and drew initiates from across the Greek and Roman world.

fun_facts.text: Line 2 contains a pun-like pair of names for pests or harms, 'Undercutter' and 'Woodcutter', whose exact meaning is uncertain.

language_notes.text: "I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I am sure."
"Undercutter" and "Woodcutter" name a harmful pest or agent of hurt; the exact reference is obscure, and the text here is corrupt.
"Like a brand" means like a burning log or piece of firewood laid in the embers.
"Winged words" is a Homeric formula for words that fly swiftly from speaker to hearer.
Swearing by the water of Styx, the river of the underworld, was the gods' most binding oath.
Refers to a ritual war among Eleusinian youths, probably commemorated in the festival honouring Demophoon.
Points to the founding of Demeter's temple at Eleusis, home of the Eleusinian Mysteries; Callichorus is a well there.
"All things without fail" means everything exactly, leaving nothing out, as Demeter had instructed them.
"Harkened" means listened and paid heed; "right speedily" means very quickly.
"Kept it hid" means Demeter held the seed concealed beneath the soil, so that nothing sprouted.
The gods would lose their "right of gifts and sacrifices" because, with no crops, humans could no longer offer them honours.
"Winged words" is a Homeric formula for speech that flies swiftly from speaker to hearer.

context_notes.text: Celeus is king of Eleusis; Metaneira is his wife. Demeter, disguised as an old woman, has become the nurse.
Ambrosia is the food of the gods, which confers or preserves immortality.
Demeter is goddess of grain and harvest, and her gift of agriculture benefits both gods and humans.
Celeus is the ruler of Eleusis. The temple built here is the sanctuary at Eleusis, the centre of the Eleusinian Mysteries.
Iris is the gods' messenger, often linked with the rainbow. Here she carries Zeus's summons to Demeter.
Zeus is called Son of Cronos because Cronos, a Titan, was his father.

literary_notes.text: Comparing the child to a brand in the fire makes the secret rite look both nurturing and alarming.
The conditional "had not" signals that Metaneira's watching will ruin the immortalising.
"Bright goddess, lovely-crowned" keeps Demeter's stately epithets even as her anger rises.
Demeter's scorn for mortals shows her divine impatience and the gap between gods and humans.
The house filled with brightness "as with lightning" conveys the overwhelming force of the goddess's revealed divinity.
The boy rejects ordinary human care, showing how much the goddess's loss costs him.
The child Demophoon's growth is compared to that of an immortal, hinting at Demeter's secret divine nurture of him.
"Rich-crowned Demeter" is a fixed descriptive epithet, and it contrasts with the barren land she causes.
The plough-drawing oxen and the wasted barley make the famine vivid by showing human effort that yields nothing.
The prospect of Demeter destroying the whole human race shows how total and dangerous her grief has become.
